props.title: Black Moon
props.initialSlug: Lawman hunts criminals using lunar superstition

sections.content: Black Moon stands as a fascinating early Hollywood exploration of Haitian Voodoo culture, though filtered through a problematic colonial lens. Directed by Roy William Neill, this pre-Code horror-thriller follows Dorothy Burgess as Juanita, a woman drawn back to her Caribbean birthplace only to become entangled in dark rituals. The film shares thematic DNA with White Zombie (1932), both capitalizing on American audiences' exotic fascination with Caribbean spirituality. While deeply problematic in its portrayal of indigenous practices, these films opened doors for later, more nuanced explorations of Vodou in cinema like The Serpent and the Rainbow (1988).

sections.content: The 1930s saw Hollywood grappling with representations of the Caribbean and its spiritual practices, often through a sensationalized lens. I Walked with a Zombie (1943) would later take a more atmospheric approach under producer Val Lewton's guidance, while Angel Heart (1987) brought voodoo themes into neo-noir territory. Black Moon stands out for its pre-Code elements, allowing more explicit content than would be permitted just months later under stricter enforcement. SUBHEAD: Colonial Gaze in Early Horror

The film's treatment of Caribbean culture reflects deeper issues of colonial representation in early Hollywood. While King Kong (1933) portrayed mysterious islands through pure fantasy, Black Moon attempted a more grounded approach, though still steeped in exoticism. This would influence later films like Live and Let Die (1973) and The Believers (1987), which continued wrestling with voodoo themes through western perspectives.
